Simplify the following powers of \(i\).

  • \(i^{21}=\)
  • \(i^{43}=\)
  • \(i^{48}=\)
  • \(i^{58}=\)

For any positive integer \(n\), we can evaluate \(i^n\) by determining the remainder when \(n\) is divided by 4.

Remainder of \(n/4\) \(i^n\)
0 \(1\)
1 \(i\)
2 \(-1\)
3 \(-i\)

In computer programming, the modulo operator returns the remainder. This operation is used so frequently, that it is often abbreviated to a single symbol (for example, in Python, 5%2 represents the remainder when 5 is divided by 2.)

I will represent the remainders using the Desmos notation.

  • \(\mathrm{mod}(21,4)=1\) so \(i^{21}=i\)
  • \(\mathrm{mod}(43,4)=3\) so \(i^{43}=-i\)
  • \(\mathrm{mod}(48,4)=0\) so \(i^{48}=1\)
  • \(\mathrm{mod}(58,4)=2\) so \(i^{58}=-1\)

To find the remainder using a scientific calculator, I would divide by 4, floor the result, multiply by 4, and subtract that amount from the original.

\[\mathrm{mod}(x,4)~=~x-4\cdot \left\lfloor\frac{x}{4}\right\rfloor\]

The solutions to \(x^{2}+{10}x-{83}=0\) can be expressed, in simplest form, as \(x=h\pm p\sqrt{q}\), where \(p\) might be imaginary. Find the values of \(h\), \(p\), and \(q\).

\(h=\)

\(p=\)

\(q=\)

Write the equation.

\[x^{2}+{10}x-{83}=0\]

Identify the coefficients.

\[a=1\] \[b=10\] \[c=-83\]

Plug numbers into the quadratic formula.

\[x = \frac{-(10)\pm\sqrt{(10)^2-4(1)(-83)}}{2(1)} \]

Simplify.

\[x = \frac{-10 \pm \sqrt{100-(-332)}}{2}\]

Simplify.

\[x = \frac{-10 \pm \sqrt{432}}{2}\]

Use prime factorization.

\[x = \frac{-10 \pm \sqrt{2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot3\cdot3\cdot3}}{2}\]

Isolate the twin factors.

\[x = \frac{-10 \pm \sqrt{2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot3\cdot3}\cdot \sqrt{3}}{2}\]

Simplify the square root of the square.

\[x = \frac{-10 \pm 2\cdot2\cdot3\cdot \sqrt{3}}{2}\]

Simplify the integer products.

\[x = \frac{-10 \pm 12\cdot \sqrt{3}}{2}\]

Split the fraction.

\[x = \frac{-10}{2} \pm \frac{12\cdot \sqrt{3}}{2}\]

Both numerators contain a factor of 2.

\[x = -5 \pm 6\sqrt{3}\]

So, \(h=-5\) and \(p=6\) and \(q=3\).

Both numerators contain a factor of 2.

So, \(h=8\) and \(p=4\) and \(q=2\).

By finding parameters \(b\) and \(c\), the same function can be expressed in standard form:

\[f(x)~=~x^2+bx+c\]

Find \(b\) and \(c\).

\(b=\)

\(c=\)

Start in factored form.

\[f(x)~=~\left[x-(-2-3\sqrt{5})\right]\cdot\left[x-(-2+3\sqrt{5})\right]\]

At this point, you can either FOIL or distribute away the inside parentheses. I think it'll be a bit cleaner to distribute the subtraction across the parentheses.

\[\left[x+2+3\sqrt{5}\right]\cdot\left[x+2-3\sqrt{5}\right]\]

But now, instead of FOIL, we need to generalize, because each factor has three terms: a linear term and two constant terms. You could probably guess that we simply multiply each of the first factor's terms by each of the second factor's terms.

\[x^2+2x-3\sqrt{5}x+2x+4-6\sqrt{5}+3\sqrt{5}x+6\sqrt{5}-45\]

Combine like terms. Opposite terms cancel each other out.

\[x^2+4x-41\]

Thus, \(b=4\) and \(c=-41\).

Define function \(f\) with equation \(f(x)~=~{4}x^{2}+{7}x-{9}\).

Evaluate \(f(-2+3i)\).

\[f(-2+3i) ~=~ 4(-2+3i)^2+7(-2+3i)-9\]

The most challenging part is squaring the complex input. Remember, raising to the power of 2 means multiplying by itself. When we multiply two complex numbers, we basically "FOIL".

\[(-2+3i)^2~\equiv~(-2+3i)(-2+3i)~\equiv~4-6i-6i+9i^2\]

Remember, \(i^2=-1\).

\[(-2+3i)^2~\equiv~4-6i-6i-9\]

Combine like terms.

\[(-2+3i)^2~\equiv~-5-12i\]

So, now return to the full expression, replacing \((-2+3i)^2\) with \(-5-12i\).

\[f(-2+3i) ~=~ 4(-5-12i)+7(-2+3i)-9\]

Distribute.

\[f(-2+3i) ~=~ -20-48i-14+21i-9\]

Combine like terms.

\[f(-2+3i) ~=~ -43-27i\]

So, type your answer as -43-27i.
